messages.body_plain:
It would help to know how you used polygonX and how R "crashed".

It is no problem to fit a patch-level covariate where patch = searched polygon. Just assign covariates(vertici) <- data.frame(soil = c(1,2,1,1,2,1,1,2)) or whatever your soil types are, one per polygon. Then use e.g. g0~soil in your model. There is no mechanism for modelling within-patch variation.

Murray

messages.subject: Questions about sex-specific estimates
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Murray for your recent fix to region.N and suggestions for
obtaining sex-specific abundance estimates.

I have a few questions about estimating abundance with a couple of the
sex-specific models.

1) I have coded sex-specific models both using male/female as a
'session' and using 'sex' as a covariate. The advantage of the 'session'
approach is that region.N gives you sex-specific abundance estimates. Is
there a way to get a total population estimate? I suppose I could use
the delta method to combine the male and female variance estimates, but
is that appropriate if some parameters are in common between sexes (so
the covariance is ^=0; e.g., g0 ~ 1, and sigma ~ sex)? Or at least close
enough?

2) With 'sex' as a covariate I used the derived() function to obtain
sex-specific density estimates. However, it appears the CIs are much
smaller than when I use 'session'. I assume that these derived density
estimates are missing some variance component? Any suggestions? In my
data it is pretty clear that the sex ratio (M:F) is 1:2 so I suspect a
model without a sex effect is going to have smaller variance so I'd
prefer to combine the M and F estimates into a total abundance estimate.

3)  The reason I'd like to use 'sex' as a covariate is that I have
surveys from different years and would like to share some parameters
across years (like having sigma different by sex but the same across
years) and I don't see how to do that using the 'session' approach -
unless I am missing some trick...  Suggestions?

Thanks,

Duane

> Thanks Murray for your recent fix to region.N and suggestions for

>
> I have a few questions about estimating abundance with a couple of the
> sex-specific models.
>
> 1) I have coded sex-specific models both using male/female as a
> 'session' and using 'sex' as a covariate. The advantage of the 'session'
> approach is that region.N gives you sex-specific abundance estimates. Is
> there a way to get a total population estimate? I suppose I could use
> the delta method to combine the male and female variance estimates, but
> is that appropriate if some parameters are in common between sexes (so
> the covariance is ^=0; e.g., g0 ~ 1, and sigma ~ sex)? Or at least close
> enough?

I don't have good intuition on the limits of the delta method, but I expect it would be good enough. Also, there is now a direct approach using contrasts that I'll demonstrate with a subset of the ovenbird data.
library(secr)
ov1 <- subset(ovenCH, session = 1)
msk <- make.mask(traps(ov1), buffer = 300, nx = 25, type = 'trapbuffer')
ofit4 <- secr.fit (ov1MF, model = list(D~session, sigma~session), mask = msk,
                   details = list(contrasts = list(session = contr.sum)))
exp(coef(ofit4)['D',-2]) * 2 # double average for 2 sexes
#        beta       lcl      ucl
# D 0.9835145 0.4710242 2.053611
See the openCR vignette <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/openCR-vignette.pdf> Section 7.8 for explanation. I haven't bothered to back-transform the SE from the log scale (more fiddly than 'exp').

>
> 2) With 'sex' as a covariate I used the derived() function to obtain
> sex-specific density estimates. However, it appears the CIs are much
> smaller than when I use 'session'. I assume that these derived density
> estimates are missing some variance component? Any suggestions? In my
> data it is pretty clear that the sex ratio (M:F) is 1:2 so I suspect a
> model without a sex effect is going to have smaller variance so I'd
> prefer to combine the M and F estimates into a total abundance estimate.
>

I don't understand - with the ovenbird data I get fairly similar CI. Maybe your data are exposing an issue I haven't seen...

# sex as covariate
ofit <- secr.fit (ov1, CL = TRUE, sigma~Sex, mask = msk)
derived(ofit, groups = 'Sex')

Just an update: John and I had a productive discussion in a side thread and I think we found the issue to my problem, which was 0’s in my variance covariance matrix and SE’s for the noneuc parameter.

The issue was related to fixing sigma at 1, which was perhaps too small for grizzly bears.. So I set it to an average sigma value for the species of 6000 and the models began to fit much better.

The working model looks like this:
csecr.hii <- secr.fit(capthist = grizzCH.d, mask = GBmask.d,detectfn = "HHN",
                       details = list(userdist = fn3), model = list(D ~ 1, noneuc ~ hii, lambda0~bk + Trap_Type),
                      start=csecr.null, fixed = list(sigma = 6000))

The final piece is interpreting what the results from the model mean. The noneuc.hii parameter (human influence index) had a negative beta value (see plot). John and I discussed that this should mean that sigma is actually larger under high human influence, i.e., a large noneuc makes things effectively closer together, shrinks the space, therefore this means in reality that sigma is larger and the animals are moving more/farther in areas of high human influence?

Hopefully this 1) can help someone else with these models, and 2) can stimulate discussion on how to interpret…

Cheers,
Clayton

messages.body_plain:
Murray can certainly answer more thoroughly or correct me, but I think the parameters associated with noneuc are fit using a log-link (with an intercept by default). The userdistance function and calls to noneuc seem to do a lot of things, but in the context of landscape resistance, if a1 = 1/(2 * sigma^2), log(cost) = a2 + a3 (z(x)+z(x'))/2 with one covariate. A call to noneuc~1 (without fixing sigma) introduces what looks like nonidentifiability of sigma and noneuc, or nonidentifiability of a1 and a2 above. Things either move farther, or spaces are closer together—many possible combinations are (equally) likely. Fitting a model with noneuc ~ covariate retains an intercept for noneuc, so same issue. So it seems like either one must be fixed (distance or a2 is known, and sigma is uncertain, or sigma is 'known' but a2 is uncertain) or the intercept must be specified as nonexistent within the model call (e.g., noneuc~covariate-1), in which case log(cost) =  a2 (z(x)+z(x'))/2. This is how it's described in the 2013 paper.  noneuc~covariate-1 probably would have been a much quicker solution!

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Thanks. Indeed, all the applications we use and the way our fitting function is set up is to drop the intercept, although recently we have considered exploring ways of/reasons to include the intercept – like those Murray has implemented (by we, I mean the Royle et al scr-connectivity paper and the Sutherland et al non-euc paper).

So, if I understand you correctly, fitting the ~X-1 model means you don’t have to assume a sigma value like Clay did? Seems like a better solution.

Regarding the cost function, and given it is the same formulation as I am familiar with (thanks for saving me the reading J), here is some behavior I found when standardizing covariate cost surfaces (this is just an fyi I found interesting, and potentially probalematic):

Basically, if d_cost = f(d_euc * cost), consider the example where the resistance parameter is positive, i.e., cost function should evaluate to > 1 and d_cost should be greater than d_euc. Good to think of just a single move from one pixel to a neighbor here, but it scales to the path. This script shows that constraint isn’t respected when the covariate is negative to positive as is the case with scaling.

I might be wrong here, so happy to be corrected!

a2 <- 0.5                    #positive cost

cov <- seq(0,3,length=20)     #some values of (c1-c2)/2 covariate values

covS <- scale(cov)           #scaled

#evaluate the toy cost function

cost1 <- exp(a2 * cov)

cost2 <- exp(a2 * covS)

#plot it

par(mfrow=c(1,2))

plot(cost1 ~ cov,ylim=c(0,5)); abline(h=1)

plot(cost2 ~ cov,ylim=c(0,5)); abline(h=1)

Murray can certainly answer more thoroughly or correct me, but I think the parameters associated with noneuc are fit using a log-link (with an intercept by default). The userdistance function and calls to noneuc seem to do a lot of things, but in the context of landscape resistance, if a1 = 1/(2 * sigma^2), log(cost) = a2 + a3 (z(x)+z(x'))/2 with one covariate. A call to noneuc~1 (without fixing sigma) introduces what looks like nonidentifiability of sigma and noneuc, or nonidentifiability of a1 and a2 above. Things either move farther, or spaces are closer together—many possible combinations are (equally) likely. Fitting a model with noneuc ~ covariate retains an intercept for noneuc, so same issue. So it seems like either one must be fixed (distance or a2 is known, and sigma is uncertain, or sigma is 'known' but a2 is uncertain) or the intercept must be specified as nonexistent within the model call (e.g., noneuc~covariate-1), in which case log(cost) =  a2 (z(x)+z(x'))/2. This is how it's described in the 2013 paper.  noneuc~covariate-1 probably would have been a much quicker solution!

The rationale for fixing sigma is on p10 of secr-noneuclidean.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-noneuclidean.pdf>; it's implied but not stated that sigma and noneuc are confounded (John's point). The default link function for noneuc is log.
I suspect Clayton's original issue could have been fixed by choosing a better start value for noneuc. Note I suppressed the intercept when emulating Chris's 2014 example in the appendix to secr-noneuclidean.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-noneuclidean.pdf>.

Hello SECR group,

I'm working on a rather large multi-session SECR analysis of small mammal trapping data (10 sessions, 4 occasions, 4600 trap sites, >380 individuals captured >680 times). The study design is a randomized complete block design with 10 blocks and 5 treatments per block, I've specified each block as a different session. The trapping array has approximately the same effort across treatments (96 traps), but the spatial arrangement of the trapping grids within the treatments varies considerably, so I've specified the trapping grid as a list of unique trapping grids for each Session. messages.subject_clean: secr.fit fails to converve in multi-session analysis despite mask.check yielding LL estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean
It's a real challenge to work with such a large design. 'mask.check' is for one session at a time; it's not telling you anything useful.

You refer to 'nonconvergence', but the real issue seems to be suitable starting values: unless you start out with a viable parameter vector, likelihood maximisation will go nowhere. I suggest you play around some more.

I've also sometimes found that NA log-likelihood with a half-normal detection function is due to a few extreme movements that are wildly unlikely with that short-tailed function. Long movements may be data errors; if real then they may be better handled with a longer-tailed function (exponential).

It may help to start with CL = TRUE to restrict the problem to suitable g0, sigma at first. Maybe there is enough between-session variation that a model homogeneous across sessions is not going to work.

I hope one of these guesses helps.
Murray

>
> You refer to 'nonconvergence', but the real issue seems to be suitable starting values: unless you start out with a viable parameter vector, likelihood maximisation will go nowhere. I suggest you play around some more.
>
> I've also sometimes found that NA log-likelihood with a half-normal detection function is due to a few extreme movements that are wildly unlikely with that short-tailed function. Long movements may be data errors; if real then they may be better handled with a longer-tailed function (exponential).
>
